newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - May 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - May 5.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Kids' free doctor visits in doubt: Free medical care for children under six, promised in the Coalition agreement and endorsed by both health ministers as a priority, seems increasingly unlikely unless the government increases its subsidy offer. Page 1.

I'm staying for at least four years, PM tells Nats: Prime Minister Jim Bolger rejected talk of a coup on Sunday and said he intended to lead the National Party for at least the next four years. Page 1.

NZ republic inevitable says Clark: Labour leader Helen Clark says it is inevitable that New Zealand will eventually become a republic, and she is setting up talks with Maoris to discuss a constitution for the time when the link with Britain is broken. Page 2.

Threat to quit party as anti-Treaty move fails: A National Party stalwart has threatened to leave the party after a remit removing the status of the Treaty of Waitangi failed to get support at National's divisional conference in Auckland at the
weekend. Page 2.

Wyllie claim incorrect says Peters: A newspaper report that said NZ First MP Tutekawa Wyllie was under investigation over his election expenses and donations was incorrect, party leader Winston Peters said on Sunday. Page 2.
No deal with ACT -- PM: Prime Minister Jim Bolger has dismissed ACT NZ leader Richard Prebble's offer to form a coalition with National if it dumps NZ First. Page 2.
Loss of favour: Maori voters are turning away from NZ First, yet still prefer Winston Peters as a political leader, a poll shows. Page 2.
Henare under fire after allegations of threat: Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare has behaved inappropriately for a minister of the Crown, Labour and the Alliance said on Sunday. Page 3.

Free trade with U.S. on agenda: International Trade Minister Lockwood Smith is to start negotiations for a free-trade agreement with the United States that he says would be a "coup" for New Zealand. Page 3.

Westpac tips big rise in unemployed: Unemployed is forecast to rise significantly to 6.5 percent from a record low of 5.9 percent in December, in the March quarter household labour force due out tomorrow. Page 16.
Tower opposes super plan: New Zealanders should not be forced into a compulsory super scheme in the next three to four years, the country's biggest savings fund company, Tower Group, said. Page 16.
ANZ predicts limited monetary easing: The Reserve Bank may be in a position to allow a further but limited easing in monetary conditions this year, ANZ Bank says. Page 16.
Papamoa supermall plan meets opposition: A Wellington developer's plan for a 200-shop supermall at Papamoa, 15 kilometres east of Mount Manganui, is already encountering opposition. Page 17.

Southland society profit slips: The Southland Building Society is expected to report a 5.5 percent fall in pre-tax profit to $7 million for the year to March 31, chief executive Ross Smith said on Sunday. Page 7.
TVNZ raises profit targets: The special $20 million bonus dividend paid by Television New Zealand to the government last year is unlikely to be repeated in a hurry. Page 18.
Tranz Rail's weak trading seen as temporary problem: Current weak trading by rail operator Tranz Rail was a temporary problem, according to Roger Armstrong at Doyle Paterson Brown. Page 18.

CanWest may be forced to dump more Ten shares: The Australian Broadcasting Authority says it may not be satisfied if Canadian media company Canwest Global Communications reduced its economic interest in the Ten Group to 57.5 percent. Page 18.
Power price goes up: Malborough Electric has announed a power price increase of just under five cents a day for the average home, to take effect from June 1. Page 18.

Exporters establish lobby voice: A rift over opposition to a $100 million business assistance programme started by the government has prompted formation of the New Zealand Exporters Confrence. Page 18.
